A B S T R A C T
A novel low alloy ultrahigh strength steel was developed by introducing extremely high-density NiAl clusters (~
4.88 × 10<sup>24</sup> m<sup>−</sup> <sup>3</sup>). The steel exhibited an ultimate tensile strength of ~ 1.9 GPa, a total elongation of ~ 15 %, a U-
notch impact absorption energy of ~ 80 J and a fracture toughness of 108 MPa⋅m<sup>1/2</sup>. The precipitation behavior
and the toughening mechanisms were systematically investigated. Highly dispersed nano-NiAl clusters and
submicron ε-carbides precipitate independently, although a small fraction of NiAl clusters interacts with Si
during precipitation, thereby increasing the availability of heterogeneous nucleation sites. NiAl clusters promote
uniform dislocation distribution, suppressing pile-ups at boundaries and delaying crack initiation. The study
revealed multi-scale toughening mechanisms, including large dimple growth, uniform plastic deformation,
secondary crack formation, and extensive crack deflection, which collectively result in a ~ 23 % improvement in
impact absorption energy. These findings demonstrate that dual-precipitation of NiAl cluster and ε-carbides and
dislocation-precipitate interactions provides an effective strategy for achieving high toughness at a tensile
strength of ~ 1.9 GPa in low alloy ultrahigh strength steels.
